sections.heading: Disadvantages of Infrared Thermal Imaging, and When a Scan Is the Right Call

runs.v: An infrared thermal scan reads temperature differences, not water, so it depends on the weather window, loses contrast under ballast, pavers, or a vegetated roof, and works best on insulated low-slope roofs; on other roof types, such as steep shingle roofs, attic ventilation and the roof structure mask the pattern. It shows the wet footprint rather than a pinhole, and pinpointing a pinhole in a membrane takes an electronic membrane test, a separate method covered by ASTM D7877. Moisture under a membrane is invisible to the naked eye, and a thermogram only suggests it, so telling wet areas from dry areas on the image still takes core cuts.

Infrared thermal imaging is particularly effective for flat or low-slope roofs: TPO and PVC membranes reflect heat and tolerate ponding water, and EPDM rubber is a cost-effective choice for low-traffic roofs, each laid over an insulated deck the camera reads well. Steep roofs are different: architectural asphalt shingles last 30 years or more, standing-seam metal can last 50 years or longer, and natural slate can last 60 to 150 years with proper maintenance at a typical installed cost of about $10 to $30 per square foot, and on those roofs a hands-on visual inspection usually finds the problem faster than a thermal scan.

c.v: Is an infrared scan worth it?

runs.v: It is the right call when a stain keeps returning away from any obvious opening, when the roof is an insulated low-slope roof, and when the alternative is exploratory tear-out. Infrared thermography is a non-destructive leak detection method that can locate roof leaks in flat and low-slope roofs and flag them before they cause wider damage, so the search narrows to verified wet areas and targeted repairs cost less than opening the roof by guesswork. Wet insulation loses most of its R-value, often described as dropping to almost zero, so timely infrared scans can also lower energy costs by keeping the insulation dry. A general home inspection with a handheld thermal camera is a different product, and a search for "roof moisture scan New Jersey NJ" returns both, so ask whether a quote includes core-cut verification.

faqs.q: How does an infrared scan find a roof leak in West Orange?

runs.v: It maps the saturated insulation below the membrane after sunset, when wet areas hold the day's warmth longer than dry areas and show as warm anomalies on the thermal image, per Fluke and IIBEC. ASTM C1153 is the standard practice for locating wet insulation in roofing systems, per ASTM and the NRCA.

faqs.q: Does infrared imaging find the exact entry point?

runs.v: No. It finds the wet footprint, which sits away from the breach because water travels through the roof assembly, so the technician traces the verified wet area back toward the flashing, seam, or penetration that admits the water, per Fluke and IIBEC.

faqs.q: Why does ASTM C1153 require a core cut?

runs.v: A thermal anomaly indicates suspected moisture rather than a diagnosis, so a core cut, probe, or calibrated moisture meter confirms the presence, depth, and extent of the moisture, per ASTM and Fluke. Verification matters most in winter, when the wet-area contrast narrows to about 5°F.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for the scan or the follow-up repair in West Orange?

runs.v: The scan is a diagnostic survey that opens nothing. Under N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7, repair work on up to 25% of the roof area in a 12-month period needs no permit, and a complete re-roof on a detached one- or two-family home is also ordinary maintenance that needs no permit; on a commercial, multi-family, or attached building, work exceeding 25% of the roof area requires a permit, so confirm with the West Orange construction office before work.

faqs.q: Can an infrared scan read any commercial membrane on the West Orange corridor?

runs.v: It reads insulated low-slope membranes such as EPDM, TPO, and modified bitumen, because the method reads the temperature pattern of the layers below; ballast lowers the contrast, so a Newark Quality Roofing technician confirms the method suits the roof before the survey. EPDM lasts 15 to 25 years, TPO 7 to 20 years, and modified bitumen 20 years, per the InterNACHI life-expectancy chart.
